# Configuration reference
Every setting in `ansible/group_vars/all.yml`, with the explanation that accompanies it in the file. Edit that file, then either `make apply` (this machine) or `make image` (a new artifact).

## Workstation Configuration
 This is the file to edit. Everything else in this repo is machinery that
 turns what is declared here into a bootable image.
 Change something, then either:
   make image    -> build a fresh image carrying the change
   make apply    -> converge THIS running machine to it, no reimage needed

### `workstation_balena_etcher_enabled`

`true`

BalenaEtcher: no apt repository exists in current vendor documentation --
checked 2026-08 against github.com/balena-io/etcher's README, which only
describes downloading a versioned .deb and running
`apt install ./balena-etcher_*_amd64.deb`. Installed that way, pinned, rather
than via apps_apt_repos, and bumped deliberately when a new version is
wanted -- the same trust model group_vars already uses for dev_mise_runtimes.

### `balena_etcher_version`

`"2.1.6"`

### `balena_etcher_release_base`

`https://github.com/balena-io/etcher/releases/download`

### `balena_etcher_deb_url`

_(list or block — see the file)_

### `balena_etcher_deb_sha256`

`2bdebb46c9f750a9abf11c188ff69a405b4a4fed114333d634c3b3fe59a64057`

From the release's combined SHA256SUMS.Linux.x64.txt. A mismatch fails the
download task outright, so an interrupted or tampered fetch stops the build
instead of installing something unverified.

### `workstation_1password_enabled`

`true`

### `apps_1password_debsig_key_id`

`AC2D62742012EA22`

1Password additionally documents a debsig-verify policy, which checks the
.deb's own signature on top of apt's repository signature. The policy lives
in a directory named after 1Password's signing key ID.
The directory name is derived from the long ID of 1Password's signing key,
and has been confirmed to match the key they publish.
Keep it checked rather than assumed: a wrong value fails silently, because
the policy lands where dpkg never looks, stays inert, and apt install
succeeds anyway. `make verify-repos` re-verifies it against the published
key, so a rotation shows up as a failure instead of as an image that
quietly stops validating the packages it installs.

### `workstation_firewall_enabled`

`true`

### `workstation_ssh_server_enabled`

### `workstation_phase`

`live`

Overridden to 'image' by Packer. Defaults to 'live' so `make apply` just works.

### `workstation_image_version`

`dev`

### `workstation_build_date`

`unknown`

### `workstation_build_user`

`packer`

Throwaway account Packer uses inside the build VM; roles/seal deletes it
before export. Declared here so the name lives in one place rather than only
in the Packer variables and the seal template's fallback.

 Three package sources, all declared as plain data. To add software, add a
 line -- no role edits required.

### `apps_apt_dev`

**APT: development**

### `apps_apt_desktop`

_(list or block — see the file)_

**APT: desktop**
Ignored entirely when workstation_desktop_enabled is false.

### `apps_apt_absent`

_(list or block — see the file)_

Packages to remove (Ubuntu ships a few things you may not want).

### `apps_apt_repos`

_(list or block — see the file)_

**APT: third-party repositories**
Each entry adds a signed keyring and a sources.list.d entry. Keys are
dearmoured to /etc/apt/keyrings, never added to the deprecated global keyring.

### `apps_snap`

`[]`

**Snap**
Empty by design. VS Code used to be installed here as a classic snap; it now
comes from Microsoft's apt repository instead (see apps_apt_repos above), and
keeping both would put two independent copies on the image, each with its own
update mechanism and its own ~300MB.

### `apps_flatpak`

_(list or block — see the file)_

**Flatpak (flathub)**

### `dev_mise_enabled`

`true`

**Language runtimes, via mise**
mise installs per-user toolchains without polluting the system, and pins
versions in one place. Set to {} to skip.

## Dotfiles
 Managed with chezmoi. The image ships the chezmoi binary only -- the repo
 is pulled on first login, so nothing personal is baked into a flashable
 artifact and the same image is safe to share or re-flash anywhere.

### `dotfiles_enabled`

`true`

### `dotfiles_repo`

`""            # e.g. https://github.com/roycohen2013/dotfiles.git`

### `dotfiles_apply_on_login`

`true`

## Desktop Settings (Gnome, Via Dconf)
 Applied for workstation_user. Values are GVariant literals, so strings need
 their own inner quotes: "'prefer-dark'".

### `desktop_dconf`

_(list or block — see the file)_

### `desktop_autologin`

`false`

Automatic login. Convenient on a personal laptop, weak on a stolen one.

### `desktop_wireshark_capture_as_user`

`true`

Let the workstation user capture packets without sudo.
wireshark-common asks this via debconf and defaults to FALSE, so an
unattended install produces a Wireshark that cannot capture as your user --
and no 'wireshark' group to join, because postinst only creates that group
when this is enabled. Setting it preseeds the answer and adds the user to
the group.
The tradeoff, in Debian's own words: dumpcap becomes setuid/setcap, which
"may be a security risk". It is still the option Debian recommends over
running the whole GUI as root. Set false to ship the stock behaviour, where
capture requires elevation.

 actually enable the power/thermal services.
